preamble: The aspirated retroflex affricate [ʈʂʰ] (pinyin ch) is fronted to the aspirated alveolar affricate [tsʰ] (pinyin c), always as part of a series-wide merger affecting zh, ch and sh together. Middle Chinese words with the retroflex initial 初 (Baxter tsrh-, [ʈʂʰ]) have [tsʰ] in Cantonese and in Southwestern Mandarin such as Chengdu Sichuanese, which have no retroflex series; in present-day Taiwanese Mandarin the same deretroflexion is pervasive in everyday speech, attributed to Southern Min substrate influence, so that ch- and c- syllables become homophonous.

examples.note: Recorded by Chung (2006: 207) in 查字 'look up a word' from a broadcaster; the retroflex initials zh, ch, sh merge into z, c, s in most Taiwan Mandarin speech.
Chung (2006: 203) notes that speakers who merge must deliberately retroflex to keep 一成 'one tenth' apart from 一層 'one layer'.
The Middle Chinese retroflex sibilants merged with the dentals in Cantonese.
Sichuanese lacks the retroflex initials [ʈʂ ʈʂʰ ʂ ʐ] of Beijing Mandarin; the whole series corresponds to dental sibilants.

sources: Chen, P. (1999). Modern Chinese: History and Sociolinguistics. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139164375
Chung, K. S. (2006). Hypercorrection in Taiwan Mandarin. Journal of Asian Pacific Communication 16(2): 197–214. https://doi.org/10.1075/japc.16.2.04chu
